A 2 kg mass is being pulled up a slope by a string of tension 10 Newtons. The slope is at an angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal and the coefficient of friction is 0.3. As well as friction, the forces of gravity \(g\) and the normal are also acting.

Copy the diagram.

By resolving forces with components along and perpendicular to the slope, find the net force \(F_{net}\) in Newtons up the slope.

questions.stem:
An object of mass \(m\) rests on a plane inclined at a variable angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal. It experiences a friction force, \(F\), and a normal force, \(N\). The friction force is \(F=\mu N\) where \(\mu\) is constant. The normal force, \(N\), is equal in magnitude to the force the object exerts on the plane perpendicular to the plane. Let \(\alpha\) be the maximal angle that the plane can be tilted before the object begins to slide down the plane.

For some \(\theta\gt\alpha\), a horizontal force \(H\) is applied to the object so that if \(H\) is sufficiently large, then the object will slide up the plane and if \(H\) is sufficiently small, then the object will slide down the plane.

Show that, for the object to remain motionless, \(H\) must satisfy \(mg\tan(\theta-\alpha)\le H\le mg\tan(\theta+\alpha)\)

steps.explain: No sliding up: the up-slope push \(H\cos\theta\) must not beat gravity plus maximum friction (friction acts down-slope).
No sliding down: gravity's slope component must not beat \(H\cos\theta\) plus maximum friction (now acting up-slope).

questions.answer: At angle α (limiting): F = mg sin α, N = mg cos α ⇒ μ = tan α. With H at angle θ: N = H sin θ + mg cos θ. No sliding up: H cos θ ≤ mg sin θ + μN = mg sin θ + tan α(H sin θ + mg cos θ); dividing by cos θ: H(1 − tan θ tan α) ≤ mg(tan θ + tan α) ⇒ H ≤ mg tan(θ + α). No sliding down: mg sin θ ≤ H cos θ + tan α(H sin θ + mg cos θ) ⇒ mg(tan θ − tan α) ≤ H(1 + tan θ tan α) ⇒ H ≥ mg tan(θ − α).

keyPoints.text: Show that, for the object to remain motionless
keyPoints.note: First get μ = tan α. Then friction can act either way: write one inequality for each direction.

questions.stem:
A body of mass 1 kg is moving in a horizontal straight line and is acted on by a force \(F=8x^3+36x\) newtons, where \(x\) is the displacement of the body in metres, measured from the origin.
If the body is initially one metre to the right of the origin with velocity of 11 m/s, find the displacement function \(x(t)\).
questions.hint: v² turns out to be a perfect square, (2x² + 9)²; then integrate dt/dx = 1/(2x² + 9).

steps.explain: Mass 1 kg, so \(\ddot x=8x^3+36x\). Use \(\ddot x=\frac{d}{dx}(\frac12v^2)\).
Take the positive root, since \(v=11\gt 0\) at \(x=1\) (and \(2x^2+9\) is never 0).

keyPoints.note: Use ẍ = d/dx(½v²); v² = (2x² + 9)². Then separate dx/dt = 2x² + 9.

questions.stem: A particle moving in a straight line has an acceleration given by \(\ddot{x}=x^2-5\) where its displacement is \(x\) metres from the origin. Initially the particle is at the origin and has velocity \(5\ \text{ms}^{-1}\). Find the velocity of this particle when it is 3 metres to the right of the origin.
questions.hint: Use ẍ = d/dx(½v²), integrate, then use x = 0, v = 5.

steps.explain: Acceleration depends on \(x\), so use \(\ddot x=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac12v^2\right)\).
The velocity started positive and \(v^2\) never reaches 0 on the way from 0 to 3 (its minimum there is about 10.1), so it stays positive: \(v=\sqrt{13}\).

keyPoints.note: ẍ is in terms of x, so write ẍ = d/dx(½v²).

questions.stem: A rocket is fired vertically from the Earth's surface with initial speed \(V\ \text{ms}^{-1}\). Assuming negligible air resistance, the acceleration experienced by the rocket is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the centre of the earth and is directed towards the centre of the Earth. Show that an expression for the velocity, \(v\), of the rocket is given by \(v^2=\dfrac{2k}{x}+V^2-\dfrac{2k}{R}\) where \(k\) is the constant of proportionality and \(R\) is the distance from the Earth's centre to the surface.
questions.answer: a = −k/x² (towards the centre). v dv/dx = −k/x² ⇒ d(v²/2)/dx = −k/x² ⇒ v²/2 = k/x + C. At x = R, v = V: C = V²/2 − k/R. So v² = 2k/x + V² − 2k/R.
questions.hint: Use \(\ddot{x}=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)\) with \(\ddot{x}=-\dfrac{k}{x^2}\) (negative: towards the Earth).

steps.explain: Acceleration is inversely proportional to \(x^2\) and directed towards the Earth (decreasing \(x\)).
Write the acceleration in terms of \(v\) and \(x\).

keyPoints.note: Use d(v²/2)/dx = acceleration and the initial condition at x = R.

questions.stem: For a rocket with \(v^2=\dfrac{2k}{x}+V^2-\dfrac{2k}{R}\), show that at the Earth's surface \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2gR^2}{x}+V^2-2gR}\), where \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity.
questions.answer: At the Earth's surface x = R the acceleration is g downwards: g = k/R², so k = gR². Substitute: v² = 2gR²/x + V² − 2gR²/R = 2gR²/x + V² − 2gR. So v = √(2gR²/x + V² − 2gR).
questions.hint: At the surface \(x=R\) the acceleration is \(g\). Use it to write \(k\) in terms of \(g\) and \(R\).

keyPoints.note: At the surface the acceleration is g, so k = gR².

meta.source: Fort St High School 2020 Trial HSC Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: A rocket has velocity \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2gR^2}{x}+V^2-2gR}\). Letting \(g=9.8\ \text{ms}^{-2}\) and the distance to the Earth's surface \(R\) be 6400 km. Determine whether a rocket fired at 12 km/s is fast enough to escape Earth's gravitational pull. Justify your answer.
options: Yes: as \(x\to\infty\), \(v^2\to V^2-2gR\approx1.9\times10^7>0\), so the rocket never stops
No: \(V^2-2gR<0\) so the rocket stops and falls back
Yes: the speed of 12 km/s is greater than 9.8 km/s
questions.hint: The rocket escapes if \(v\) never reaches 0, i.e. \(v^2>0\) even as \(x\to\infty\). Use consistent units (metres and seconds).

steps.explain: Since \(v^2\) stays positive for every \(x\), the rocket never stops: it escapes (escape speed \(\sqrt{2gR}\approx11.2\) km/s) → A

keyPoints.note: Escape if v² stays positive as x → ∞.

questions.stem: Assume that the tides rise and fall in simple harmonic motion. At low tide the depth of water in a harbour was 6 m deep, and at high tide it was 10 m deep. Low tide was at 8:00 am and the high tide following it was at 3:00 pm.

parts.stem: What is the amplitude of the motion?

questions.stem:
The Covid-19 1.5 metre rule is based on the premise that a person emits droplets from a height 1.8 m above ground at an angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal so that the maximum range on the ground is 1.5 metres. Show that the maximum speed \(V\) m/s of the droplets launched is given by

\(V=\sqrt{\frac{15g}{22}}\).  (Assume there is no air resistance.)

[Hint: you can assume which angle gives the maximum range…..]
questions.hint: Use θ = 45°, write x(t) and y(t) from height 1.8, then put x = 1.5, y = 0.

steps.explain: Set up axes with the origin on the ground directly below the mouth. Using the hint, take the angle for maximum range, \(\theta=45^\circ\).
Integrate with the initial conditions \(\dot x=V\cos\theta\), \(\dot y=V\sin\theta\), \(x=0\), \(y=1.8\) at \(t=0\).
The droplet lands at \(x=1.5\), \(y=0\). Find the time from \(x\).

questions.answer: Take θ = 45° (maximum range). With the origin on the ground below the mouth: \(x=Vt\cos\theta=\frac{Vt}{\sqrt2}\), \(y=1.8+Vt\sin\theta-\frac{gt^2}{2}=1.8+\frac{Vt}{\sqrt2}-\frac{gt^2}{2}\). The droplet lands at x = 1.5, y = 0: \(t=\frac{1.5\sqrt2}{V}\), so \(0=1.8+1.5-\frac{g}{2}\cdot\frac{4.5}{V^2}\), i.e. \(3.3=\frac{2.25g}{V^2}\), \(V^2=\frac{2.25g}{3.3}=\frac{15g}{22}\), so \(V=\sqrt{\frac{15g}{22}}\).

keyPoints.text: from a height 1.8 m above ground
keyPoints.note: Start y at 1.8 (not 0). Use θ = 45° and the landing point x = 1.5, y = 0.

questions.answer: The particle reaches the wall if its height at x = d is non-negative: d tanα − g d² sec²α/(2V²) ≥ 0 ⇒ tanα ≥ g d sec²α/(2V²) ⇒ 2V² sinα cosα ≥ g d ⇒ sin2α ≥ gd/V². Since gd/V² < 1, sin⁻¹(gd/V²) = 2β exists with 0 < 2β < π/2, and sin2α ≥ sin2β holds for 2β ≤ 2α ≤ π − 2β, i.e. β ≤ α ≤ π/2 − β.
questions.hint: Strike the wall means the height at \(x=d\) is not below the ground: \(y\geq0\) when \(x=d\). Simplify to a condition on \(\sin2\alpha\).

steps.explain: Since \(d<\dfrac{V^2}{g}\), \(\dfrac{gd}{V^2}<1\), so \(2\beta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{gd}{V^2}\right)\) is defined with \(0<2\beta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\sin2\beta=\dfrac{gd}{V^2}\).

keyPoints.note: Height at \(x=d\) is non-negative leads to \(\sin2\alpha\geq\dfrac{gd}{V^2}\).

questions.stem: Frank decides to go bungee-jumping. Frank falls, from rest, off a bridge attached by an elastic cable of length \(l\) metres. After Frank falls \(l\) metres he is slowed by the cable which exerts a force of \(mgk(x-l)\), where \(m\) is his mass in kilograms, \(g\) is the constant acceleration due to gravity in \(\text{ms}^{-2}\), \(k\) is the constant of proportionality. Let \(x\) m be the distance Frank has fallen and let \(v\ \text{ms}^{-1}\) be his speed at \(x\). There is negligible air resistance for the duration of Frank's jump. Show that \(v^2=2gx-kg(x-l)^2\) for \(x>l\).
questions.answer: For x > l, net downward force: mg − mgk(x − l), so ẍ = g − gk(x − l). v dv/dx = g − gk(x − l) ⇒ ½v² = gx − ½gk(x − l)² + C. At x = l, free fall from rest gave v² = 2gl, so ½(2gl) = gl − 0 + C ⇒ C = 0. Hence v² = 2gx − gk(x − l)².
questions.hint: Net force on Frank (taking downward as positive): weight \(mg\) down and the cable force \(mgk(x-l)\) up. Use \(\ddot{x}=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}\).

steps.explain: Free fall for the first \(l\) metres: \(v^2=2gl\) at \(x=l\) (from rest).

keyPoints.note: Net force = weight minus cable force; integrate with v dv/dx.

questions.stem: Frank's speed satisfies \(v^2=2gx-kg(x-l)^2\) for \(x>l\). Show that Frank's fall is first halted at \(x=l+\dfrac{1}{k}+\sqrt{\dfrac{2l}{k}+\dfrac{1}{k^2}}\).
questions.answer: Halted: v = 0 ⇒ 2gx = kg(x − l)² ⇒ k(x − l)² − 2(x − l) − 2l = 0 (using x = (x − l) + l). Solve for x − l: x − l = [2 ± √(4 + 8kl)]/(2k) = [1 ± √(1 + 2kl)]/k. Take the positive root (x > l): x = l + 1/k + √(1/k² + 2l/k).
questions.hint: Set \(v=0\) and substitute \(u=x-l\) to get a quadratic in \(u\).

steps.explain: The positive root (the cable is stretched, \(x>l\)): \(x=l+u=l+\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac{\sqrt{1+2kl}}{k}\).

keyPoints.note: Set \(v=0\) and solve the quadratic in \(x-l\).
